name: C-Metric Accelerating Black Holes
description: An exact vacuum solution describing two black holes that accelerate away from each other, driven by a cosmic string or a strut along their axis of symmetry. With the acceleration set to zero it is the Schwarzschild black hole.
history: Tullio Levi-Civita found the static form of this spacetime in 1918 [griffiths2009, bini2004]. A year earlier Hermann Weyl had reduced every static vacuum field with an axis of symmetry to a single potential obeying Laplace's equation in an auxiliary flat space of three dimensions, and the C-metric, in its static region, is one of those fields [weyl1917, griffiths2006]. Weyl found it independently in 1919, Ezra Newman and Louis Tamburino in 1961, and Ivor Robinson and Andrzej Trautman in 1962, among their spherical gravitational waves [weyl1919, newman1961, robinson1962, griffiths2009, bini2004]. Jürgen Ehlers and Wolfgang Kundt named it the C-metric in their 1962 review of exact solutions [ehlerskundt1962, griffiths2009].¶William Kinnersley and Martin Walker first interpreted it, in 1970, as the field of a uniformly accelerating point mass, and they gave the mass a charge, so that their solution generalizes the Reissner-Nordström black hole of general relativity and Max Born's uniformly accelerated charge of classical electrodynamics [kinnersley1970, griffiths2009]. In their solution the force that accelerates the mass is a nodal singularity on a timelike surface of two dimensions, running from the particle's world line out to infinity [kinnersley1970]. They found its maximal analytic extension, whose horizons closely resemble those of the Reissner-Nordström black hole apart from one more Killing horizon due to the acceleration, and computed the pattern of the electromagnetic and gravitational waves it radiates [kinnersley1970]. Jerzy Plebański and Marek Demiański wrote down in 1976 a family of solutions for a rotating, charged, and uniformly accelerating mass, and the C-metric is its member with no rotation and no charge [plebanski1976].¶Frederick Ernst transformed the charged C-metric in 1976 into a solution in which an external electric field accelerates the charged particle [ernst1976]. When the particle's equations of motion are satisfied, the nodal singularity disappears [ernst1976]. Abhay Ashtekar and Tevian Dray showed in 1981 that, for parameters in suitable intervals, the vacuum C-metric has a conformal completion whose null infinity has spherical cross sections, so Hermann Bondi's definitions of radiated energy apply to it [ashtekar1981]. Its Bondi news is nonzero, as is the electromagnetic radiation field of the charged C-metric, so Einstein's equations have exact solutions that radiate in the sense of Bondi, Rainer Sachs, and Roger Penrose [ashtekar1981]. William Bonnor studied the sources of the vacuum C-metric in 1983, reading Weyl's coordinates as cylindrical coordinates in a flat auxiliary space [bonnor1983, griffiths2006]. In that space the potential is built from the distances to three points on the axis: the two ends of the black hole horizon and the end of the acceleration horizon [griffiths2006].¶Fay Dowker, Jerome Gauntlett, David Kastor, and Jennie Traschen generalized the C-metric in 1994 to a pair of oppositely charged black holes coupled to a dilaton and accelerating uniformly, and placed them in a magnetic field, generalizing the Ernst metric of Einstein-Maxwell theory [dowker1994]. Choosing the parameters to remove the nodal singularities, and restricting them further for a weak enough coupling to the dilaton, they obtained instantons for the pair production of dilaton black holes in a magnetic field [dowker1994]. In 1995 Stephen Hawking and Simon Ross took from the C-metric the instanton for a cosmic string that breaks by creating a pair of black holes, computed its probability, and showed that only topologically unstable strings can break [hawking1995]. Douglas Eardley, Gary Horowitz, David Kastor, and Jennie Traschen showed the same year that a topologically stable string can appear to break when the spatial topology of the universe is nontrivial, and bounded the rate from below with the Euclidean C-metric [eardley1995]. Ruth Gregory and Mark Hindmarsh constructed, also in 1995, two metrics for Abelian Higgs vortices ending on black holes, in which the fields of the vortex smooth out the nodal singularities, and estimated the rate at which a string splits as negligible for strings formed at the scale of grand unification [gregory1995].¶Kenneth Hong and Edward Teo found in 2003 a form of the metric whose structure function factorizes as $(1 - x^2)(1 + 2\alpha mx)$ [hong2003]. Its roots place the two halves of the axis at $x = \pm 1$ and, with $y = 1/(\alpha r)$, the acceleration horizon at $y = 1$ and the black hole horizon at $y = 1/(2\alpha m)$ [hong2003, griffiths2006]. In the coordinates Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský gave in 2005 for accelerating and rotating black holes, the C-metric is the case without rotation or charge [griffiths2005, griffiths2006]. With Pavel Krtouš they built from those coordinates in 2006 extensions of the Kruskal-Szekeres kind across both horizons, the black hole's at $r = 2m$ and the acceleration horizon at $r = 1/\alpha$, drew conformal diagrams of two dimensions, and combined them into a picture in three dimensions of the causal structure outside the black hole horizons [griffiths2006]. They showed that the conical singularity can be removed from either half of the axis but not from both: with the angle about the axis running over $2\pi/(1 + 2\alpha m)$, which makes the half between the black holes regular, the other half carries the deficit angle $8\pi\alpha m/(1 + 2\alpha m)$, a cosmic string under tension that runs from each black hole out to conformal infinity and accelerates it, and the choice that makes that half regular puts a strut between the black holes [griffiths2006]. In a null tetrad adapted to their coordinates the only nonzero curvature component is $\Psi_2 = -m(1/r + \alpha\cos\theta)^3$, which at $\alpha = 0$ is Schwarzschild's $-m/r^3$, so the spacetime is of type D [griffiths2006].

related.text: The C-metric with the acceleration eased off to zero, $\alpha = 0$ [griffiths2006].
The C-metric is one of Robinson and Trautman's solutions, of type D like Schwarzschild's [robinson1962, griffiths2009].
The conical singularity along the axis of the C-metric is a cosmic string under tension, and it pulls the black holes apart [kinnersley1970, griffiths2006].
A black hole with a string through it on both sides, which pull equally, so the hole stays at rest [aryal1986, achucarro1995].
A magnetic field along the axis can do the pulling in place of the string. Frederick Ernst showed in 1976 that it removes the nodal singularity of the charged C-metric [ernst1976].
Tullio Levi-Civita found the static form of the C-metric in 1918, a year before his field of a line of mass [griffiths2009, levicivita1919].
An accelerating spacetime of type D with a regular axis. It needs no string, since the recoil of the light it shines does the pushing [podolsky2008].
A black hole with a spin and a cosmological constant where this one has an acceleration. Plebański and Demiański put all three into one family of solutions [kamran2009, plebanski1976].

A black hole with a spin where this one has an acceleration. Plebański and Demiański's family holds both, and Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský wrote it in 2005 in a form that is Kerr's metric with no acceleration and the C-metric with no rotation [plebanski1976, griffiths2005].

The charged black hole at rest. William Kinnersley and Martin Walker gave the accelerating mass a charge in 1970, and the horizons of their solution resemble Reissner-Nordström's, with one more for the acceleration [kinnersley1970].

The charged black hole of string theory. Fay Dowker, Jerome Gauntlett, David Kastor, and Jennie Traschen wrote the C-metric for a pair of them in 1994, oppositely charged and accelerating apart [dowker1994].

A rotating black hole with a NUT parameter and no acceleration. Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský's form of the Plebański-Demiański family reduces to it when the acceleration is switched off, and to the C-metric when the spin and the twist are [griffiths2005].
Two black holes of opposite charge at rest on one axis. Emparan placed that pair on top of the barrier under which a magnetic field creates the accelerating pair [emparan2000].

The anti-Nariai universe has a C-metric of its own. Óscar Dias and José Lemos found it in 2003 as a limit toward a degenerate horizon of the accelerating black holes with a negative cosmological constant [dias2003].
Classes A and B of the table Ehlers and Kundt put the C-metric in. Their fields admit an isotropy group, and the fields of class C admit none [ehlerskundt1962, bicak2009].
A static black hole bent by matter far away, with nothing on its axis. Its horizon is smooth all the way round, with no string or strut to meet [fairhurst2001].
A spinning hole in Bertotti and Robinson's magnetic field. Its static member is the one that does not accelerate in a family that also holds the C-metric set in that field [ovcharenko2026].

The C-metric in anti-de Sitter space, cut along its surface $x = 0$ where a brane sits. By holography the metric on the brane is a black hole of three dimensions with quantum fields around it [emparan2000branes2, emparan2020qbtz].

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, which is a length; the black hole horizon sits at $r = 2m$
Acceleration, an inverse length, with $2\alpha m < 1$; the acceleration horizon sits at $r = 1/\alpha$
A pure number scaling the angle about the axis; $C = 1/(1 + 2\alpha m)$ makes the half axis $\theta = 0$ regular and leaves a cosmic string along $\theta = \pi$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates of Jerry Griffiths, Pavel Krtouš, and Jiří Podolský, $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r - 2m\right)\left(\alpha^3\,r^3\,m\cos\theta + \alpha^2\,r^3 - \alpha^2\,r^2\,m + \alpha\,r^2\cos\theta - 3\alpha\,r\,m\cos\theta - m\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)}{r^3\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{2\alpha^3\,r^4\cos\theta - 3\alpha^3\,r^3\,m\cos\theta + \alpha^2\,r^3 - \alpha^2\,r^2\,m - \alpha\,r^2\cos\theta + \alpha\,r\,m\cos\theta - m}{r\left(r - 2m\right)\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{2\alpha\,r\sin\theta}{1 + \alpha r\cos\theta}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{\left(2m - r\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)}{\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{C^2\left(2m - r\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{1 + \alpha r\cos\theta}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{\alpha\left(r - 2m\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)\sin\theta}{r^2\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{\alpha\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)\sin\theta}{\left(r - 2m\right)\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)\left(1 - \alpha^2r^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{2}{r\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{\alpha\left(3\alpha\,r\,m\cos\theta + r + m\right)\sin\theta}{\left(1 + \alpha r\cos\theta\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{C^2\left(\alpha^2\,r\,m\cos^3\theta + \alpha^2\,r\,m\cos\theta + \alpha\,r + 3\alpha\,m\cos^2\theta - \alpha\,m + \cos\theta\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m\cos\theta\right)\sin\theta}{1 + \alpha r\cos\theta}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates of Kenneth Hong and Edward Teo, $(\tau, y, x, \phi)$, all dimensionless and related to the spherical coordinates by $\tau = \alpha ct$, $y = 1/(\alpha r)$, and $x = \cos\theta$.
